series: Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 4.1 · October 2026
title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow

slides.title: Reward the Stock as Well as the Flow
slides.subtitle: Notional capitalized value and guarantee-based climate incentives
slides.message: Credit each country with a balance opened by its carbon stock and debited for every tonne emitted above an allowance. Use it as guarantee capacity on green borrowing, not cash: on the development banks' record each dollar of expected loss buys about $80 of interest saving.
slides.author: Stephen J. Stretton · writing in a personal capacity

slides.title: The proposal: a climate balance that the stock opens and emissions draw down

points.text: verified carbon stock × a low stock price.
debited at a uniform debit price for every tonne emitted above an agreed allowance; credited for every tonne below.
the balance caps the guarantees development banks provide on the country's green borrowing, backed by a buffer held in a trust.
no sovereign pays a fine for emitting, but it can lose part of a balance it counts as its own. Fixed at entry, the balance cannot be raised by threatening to clear.

slides.source: Working paper 4.1, Section 4; Stretton, Time and Chance, ch. 21; Harstad (2016).

slides.title: A guarantee is worth many times what it costs the guarantor

points.text: 0.77% defaults a year, 95.1% recovered. At a 3-point spread, about $80 saved per $1 of expected loss.
the country gives up, about $27.
(no preferred-creditor status; 3% calls, 37% loss): 2.7, or 1.9 net.

slides.source: GEMs (2025); Longstaff et al. (2011); Cruces and Trebesch (2013); working paper 4.1, Proposition 1.

slides.title: Use two prices: a low one sizes the balance, a uniform one prices each tonne

points.text: at $100/t Guyana's stock is a $1.95tn balance that never binds, so a tonne costs nothing; sized to $5bn of borrowing, a tonne costs 15 cents.
stock at $0.26/t opens $5bn; a $50 debit makes each tonne cost the country about $30 (= $50 × 3% ÷ 5%).

points.lead: Baselines stop mattering at the margin:
points.text: the allowance changes how much a country gets, not how hard each tonne is rewarded.
capacity must bind and the scheme must have no end date; surplus balance flows to a trust account.

slides.title: Big incentives need borrowers, not big donations
slides.note: At a 3-point spread saving. Strong for large, lower-rated borrowers; weak for investment-grade ones (1 point), who are better served by interest on the balance in a trust account. Multilateral forest funds pledged about $400m a year from 2008.
slides.source: Working paper 4.1, Table 5; GEMs (2025); TFFF Concept Note 3.0 (2025).

slides.title: Capacity that declines as technology gets cheaper pays for acting now, at half the cost

points.text: a $1bn reform cutting 5 Mt a year needs $20/t to act now ($32–37 with uncertainty).
halves the donor cost: $25m to $13m on the record ($740m to $370m stress).
the same incentive would cost $1bn.

slides.source: Author's calculation; Dixit and Pindyck (1994); working paper 4.1, Proposition 3 and Figure 2.

slides.title: The risks are real but can be bounded

points.text: capacity is capped, only green borrowing is covered, and a call becomes a debt to a development bank.
the host's liability shrinks but stays its own, and other creditors may charge more. Size the buffer to stressed losses and publish it.
if guarantees consumed IBRD-style capital (18%) instead of a held buffer, the ratio would fall from 80 to about 7.5.
worth a low price, not none: the balance is cheap capacity, makes the debit enforceable and leaves the margin to the debit price.

slides.source: Working paper 4.1, Sections 6.7 and 8; Chamon et al. (2022); World Bank (2024).
